newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy faces tough task after 1996 budget overshoot.
newsitem.headline: Italy faces tough task after 1996 budget overshoot.

text.p: Italy faces a monumental task in 1997 to bring its public finances to heel and secure a berth in European economic and monetary union (EMU) ahead of its launch in two years' time, economists said on Friday.

The scale of the challenge was spelt out in cold print on Thursday when the Treasury announced Italy had run a 1996 public sector deficit of 138.50 trillion lire ($90.5 billion) -- well ahead of a revised government target of 123 trillion lire.
That means the government has to cut the deficit from around 7.5 percent of gross domestic product to three percent in just one year to be sure of qualifying as a founder member of a currency union.
"Yesterday's figures were very disappointing. With 1997 a crunch year in relation to EMU, Italy is not in a very strong position," said Ken Wattret, an economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London.

The odds were shortening on the government having to push through a supplementary budget early in 1997 fast on the heels of a 62.5 trillion lire deficit-cutting package passed by parliament at the end of the year, analysts said.
The 1997 deficit figures will be used as a basis to decide who joins an advance party of currency union members in 1999.

"If the figures are confirmed, it will be almost impossible to cut the deficit in half in one year, bearing in mind that the economy is stagnating," said Carmen Nuzzo, economist at Salomon Brothers in London.

The government put a brave face on the figures, which had been widely expected, saying it would not be deflected from its path. "It's nothing that we had not forecast. We will stick to our line," said Deputy Prime Minister Walter Veltroni.

Economists said the 1996 deficit looked particularly bad because for once the government had not indulged in a traditional end-of-year ritual of "window-dressing" -- using accounting tricks to make the figures look better than they are.

The deficit numbers were also swollen by local authorities drawing heavily on their accounts with the Treasury in the closing weeks of 1996 in anticipation of a tight squeeze on spending in the year just begun.

"The administrations of the main cities, informed of the government's intention...to put a brake on their withdrawals from the Treasury, hurried up and took the cash," said the Milan business daily Il Sole 24 Ore.
The government will face an agonising choice in the early months of 1997 whether to bite the fiscal bullet even harder and force a fresh round of belt-tightening on a tax-harried public.
"There is a need for an extra budget to address the overshoot (in 1996) and because the government's 1997 figures are over-optimistic," said Wattret.
A trades union leader said the government would have to weigh up the situation at the end of the first quarter.

"News of an increase in the state borrowing requirement is worrying. But I think we will have to wait until March or April to have a clearer picture," said Sergio Cofferati, Secretary General of the CGIL trade union confederation.
Italian bond prices, which have soared in recent months in anticipation that Italy will join EMU, did not flinch despite the bad news.
Some analysts expect a sell-off in the market if, as expected, the Bank of Italy cuts interest rates sharply in the coming weeks.
"But it will prove temporary," said Nuzzo. "The government is going in the right direction but the adjustment is slower than hoped."
